subtype: Approach: audit of privacy settings and old posts [Action]
passage: Bidisha, I'll tell you what I did last Sunday, because it took only an hour. I'm Mridula, the sensible girl in our lane according to the aunties, and my cousin, who works in tech and says she reviews hers monthly, told me to look at my account the way a stranger would. So I did. First, tags: three photos where friends had tagged me with our club's full name. I asked them to remove it. Then location: I switched it off in every app, because my posts basically told anyone when I'm at tuition. Then I scrolled far down to a photo from Class Eight: me in uniform at the school gate, the name board behind me. I deleted it. Anyone could work out where I'll be at eight in the morning. Nothing scary has happened. But now nothing about my routine is public.

qa.a: Mridula deleted a photo from Class Eight of her in uniform at the school gate with the name board behind her.

qa.q: Why did Mridula switch off location?
qa.a: She was worried that her posts told anyone when she was at tuition, so strangers could work out her routine.

qa.q: What else could Mridula do to protect her account?
qa.a: She could check who follows her, keep the account private and repeat the review every few months, since old posts pile up.

qa.q: How might Mridula's friends feel when asked to remove tags?
qa.a: They may feel surprised at first, but most would understand since Mridula explains it is about privacy, not about them.

grounding: A teen reviews tags, location sharing and public photos, removes an old post showing the school gate and uniform and switches off location.

subtype: Approach: audit of privacy settings and old posts [Action]
passage:
I'm Salma. Vasudha and I were on her bed on Sunday afternoon when she said, “I'm doing a clean-up,” and turned her phone so I could watch.
She went through her account like a detective. First the tags: she removed herself from two group photos someone else had posted publicly. Then settings: she switched on approval for tags, so nobody can tag her without her saying yes. Then location: she turned off location sharing on the app and on her camera too, so photos wouldn't carry it.
Then she scrolled right back to Class Seven. There was an old post of her at the school gate, in uniform, with the school's name clear on the board behind her. She stared at it for a moment and deleted it. “Anyone could work out where I am at eight every morning,” she said.
It took about forty minutes. She looked relieved when she was done, I think.

qa.q: What did the old post show?
qa.a: Vasudha at the school gate, in uniform, with the school's name clear on the board behind her.

qa.q: Why did Vasudha delete the Class Seven post?
qa.a: She felt uneasy seeing how clearly it showed her routine, worried anyone could work out where she is at eight every morning.

qa.q: What else could Vasudha add to the clean-up?
qa.a: Show a parent the new settings, and repeat the check every few months, since old posts and new tags pile up.

qa.q: How does the clean-up look to Salma?
qa.a: Salma sees a careful, detective-like check and thinks Vasudha looked relieved, though Salma can't be sure.

grounding: A friend watches a teen review tags, location sharing and public photos, delete an old post showing her school gate and uniform, and switch off location.

subtype: Approach: audit of privacy settings and old posts [Action]
passage:
Friday: Tanuja's cousin Lavanya, visiting from Chennai, scrolls through Tanuja's public account and frowns. “This one shows your school bag with the name on it. And this one has your building's number.”
Saturday: Tanuja sits down with her laptop. She switches the account to private. She turns off location sharing in the app and in her camera settings. She sets tagging so no one can tag her without approval, and untags herself from a stranger's public post from a school event.
Sunday: She goes through old posts one by one. She deletes a picture from two years ago of her in uniform outside the school gate, and archives three others showing the building. She shows her mother the new settings, and her mother asks her to check them again every few months.
Monday: Lavanya scrolls again and nods. “Now I'd have to be your friend to see any of it."

qa.q: What did Lavanya notice in one photo on Friday?
qa.a: Tanuja's school bag with the name on it.

qa.q: How might Tanuja have felt when Lavanya frowned on Friday?
qa.a: Tanuja was probably startled and uneasy, not having noticed how much the posts gave away.

qa.q: What else could Tanuja do to keep her account safe?
qa.a: Check new photos before posting for names, numbers or uniforms, not just clean up old ones.

qa.q: How does the account look to Lavanya on Monday?
qa.a: Lavanya is satisfied, since strangers can no longer see Tanuja's posts or work out her routine.

grounding: Shows a teen switching off location, controlling tags and deleting an old post showing her school gate and uniform so strangers cannot find her routine.
